records.title: Portfolio Site
records.abstract: The works are shown as game cases on a shelf. Pick one and press Enter: the figure carries the disc to the console, the monitor reads it and the work's page opens. The site is built on RhineLabUI, an open-source 3D archive interface by LBEILC, which I kept for the shelf and the drag controls. The cases, console, monitor, figure animations and boot sequence are my additions, modelled with Blender scripts.
findings: The shelf, the glass materials and the drag controls come from RhineLabUI.
The game case, console and monitor are generated by Blender scripts in art/, so the models can be rebuilt from source.
All of the upstream project's IP references were removed. The music and sound effects are synthesized in code.

records.title: LOCKDOWN
records.en: A 20-day survival game about cooking for a family in lockdown
records.abstract: LockDown is a survival game set in one apartment during a 20-day city lockdown. Each morning a supply package arrives, and by Day 7 it may be just noodles, a cabbage and rice. Cooking is a tangram puzzle: you cut the ingredients, fit them into a pan that is too small, and store the leftovers in a fridge where food rots. The family and the neighbours reach you through the phone. Based on my family's lockdown in Shanghai in 2022.
findings: Twelve ingredients, each a shape of 3 to 7 cells, are cut and fitted into a pan of 18 to 25 cells.
The fridge is a 6 by 8 grid. From Day 8, food stored for two days starts to rot, and the rot spreads to neighbouring cells.

The phone has a newspaper, a building group chat and a family chat. On Day 4 the building asks about medicine, on Day 5 the paper reports refills running late, and the same morning Grandpa's box is empty.

gallery.caption: Cut ingredients going into the pan

study.pitch: A survival game about one apartment and twenty days of lockdown. Each day you cook whatever the supply package brings by fitting ingredient shapes into a pan, store the leftovers in a fridge that can rot, and deal with the family and the neighbours on the phone.

sections.heading: The 2022 lockdown
body: LockDown is about slowly losing control while you wait for something with no announced end. The idea comes from my family's 2022 lockdown in Shanghai. We ate whatever came in the supply package, my grandparents needed medicine that nobody was allowed to go and get, and nobody told us when it would end.

I use those memories as design rules. The player receives supplies instead of shopping. The apartment never grows. Food, medicine and the neighbors' requests all come out of one small reserve. The run lasts twenty days, but the screen shows the day number with no countdown.

The cooking puzzle starts from the traditional Chinese tangram. Here the shapes are ingredients and the space is a pan or a fridge, and the gaps and leftovers show the shortage without a line of dialogue.
sections.summary: In 2022 my family was locked down at home in Shanghai. We ate what came in the supply packages, and my grandparents ran low on medicine that nobody was allowed to go out and buy. LockDown turns that into rules: no shopping, only packages; one apartment that never changes; twenty days with no countdown on the screen.

media.caption: Day 12 in the apartment.

sections.heading: A day
body: Each morning starts with yesterday's consequences. Everyone loses 2 morale and 1 health, the fridge is checked for rot, and a package arrives. By Day 7 the bag can be just noodles, a cabbage and some rice.

The player reads the phone, plans the meal, fits the food into the pan and serves it. Leftovers go into the fridge if they fit and are lost if they don't. Before Day 3 there is no fridge, and only the largest leftover keeps on the counter. Sleep moves the day on but resets nothing.

media.caption: The daily loop, from the GDD.
The Day 7 package: noodles, a cabbage and rice for three people.
Day 1 morning, with the first package waiting to be picked up.
Day 6, after dinner.

sections.summary: A day starts with the costs of the day before: everyone loses 2 morale and 1 health, the fridge is checked for rot, and a package arrives at the door. By Day 7 it can be just noodles, a cabbage and some rice. You read the phone, cook, serve, and put what is left in the fridge. Then you sleep.

sections.heading: The pan
body: I built the game around a pan rather than a resource screen, because every problem in the house ends up at dinner. A resource screen would turn Grandpa's tablets into a number. The pan turns them into a space that is too small.

The twelve ingredients are shapes of 3 to 7 cells, each with its own calories and nutrients. A cabbage is a five-cell cross worth 25 kcal, and pork takes seven cells and gives 250. A meal is scored against a 470 kcal target: 38% balance, 24% calories, 20% total nutrients and 18% pan filled. Under 42% nobody recovers health, and under 28% everyone gets weaker.

Until Day 6 there is no knife, so the pan is a plain rectangle and every piece goes in whole. After that the pan is an irregular shape of roughly 18 to 25 cells, always with a solid 3 by 3 core so the largest piece fits. The knife cuts along the grid, and the part you don't cook goes to the fridge.

media.caption: The meal screen: shapes on the left, the pan, the fridge, and the 470 kcal target.
Day 6: the new knife splits a piece of tofu along the grid.
Before the knife, whole pieces fill a plain rectangular pan.
Later, pork, tofu and egg share an irregular pan.

sections.summary: Twelve ingredients, each a tangram-style shape of 3 to 7 cells, go into the pan. A meal is scored against a 470 kcal target: 38% for balance, 24% for calories, 20% for nutrients and 18% for how full the pan is. There is no knife until Day 6, so early on every piece goes in whole. After that you can cut along the grid, and the pan becomes an irregular shape of 18 to 25 cells.

sections.heading: The fridge
body: Each new rule arrives through something in the house. On Day 1 the fridge is broken, and the next day Aunt Li complains in the building group about Grandpa dragging it around at midnight. On Day 3 he gets it working and storage unlocks. After two days of cooking everything at once, the player knows what a fridge is for.

The fridge is a 6 by 8 grid. On Day 7 the building loses power, and from Day 8 anything stored for two days grows a rotten cell. Each morning a rotten cell spreads to the next cell of the same item 62% of the time and into a touching item 35% of the time.

Rot never deletes food. The good cells can still be cooked, or cut away from the bad ones. The grade ignores rot on purpose. Every rotten cell in the pan costs each person 4 health, up to 14 a meal, so an S meal with rot in it still makes the family ill.

media.caption: The fridge on Day 8, with rot crossing between items where they touch.
Day 3: Grandpa says to put spare food in the fridge.
The repaired fridge on Day 3: 48 empty cells.

sections.summary: The fridge is broken on Day 1. Grandpa fixes it on Day 3, and from then on leftovers go into a 6 by 8 grid. On Day 7 the power goes out, and from Day 8 anything stored for two days grows a rotten cell that spreads each morning. Rotten cells can still be cooked, but each one in the pan costs every person 4 health.

sections.heading: The household
body: In 2022 there were five of us at home. For the game I cut the household to three: Grandpa, whose health depends on things from outside, Daughter, who says out loud what everyone feels, and the player, with no name or face, who makes the decisions. Director Zhang, Mr. Wang, Aunt Li, Uncle Yu and the 6F Stranger reach the flat through the building chat.

Grandpa starts on 60 health and loses 5 more every morning until his medicine is secured. On Day 5 his last box is empty. Aunt Li checks her own drawer, and half the time her strip is empty too. The 6F Stranger can get the pills sooner for two things from the fridge, and the chat names the two the game took.

On Day 8 Daughter has a fever of 38.2. A warm meal from a fridge item gives her 25 health, and letting her rest costs her 20. On Day 13 Zhang asks for food for the sealed seventh floor. On Day 18 taking Daughter downstairs early works 60% of the time, and if the patrol stops them, everyone loses 12 morale.

media.caption: Day 5: the 6F Stranger takes two fridge items for the medicine.
Day 13: the seventh floor is sealed and asks for food.
Day 8: Daughter has a fever, and the player chooses porridge.
Day 18: take Daughter downstairs early, or wait for the assigned time.

sections.summary: Three people live in the apartment: Grandpa, Daughter and the player. Grandpa needs medicine and loses 5 health every morning until it is found. On Day 5 his last box runs out, and a stranger on the sixth floor offers pills in exchange for two items from the fridge. Daughter gets a fever on Day 8. Five neighbours talk to you through the building group chat.

sections.heading: The phone
body: The phone has three channels at three distances: the city newspaper, the building group and the family chat. Often they cover the same problem. On Day 4 Zhang asks every flat for its medicine doses, on Day 5 the paper reports refills running late, and that morning Grandpa finds his box empty.

The HUD shows the day and each person's health. After dinner one family member answers in a single line, the weakest one when the meal went badly, and that is how the player learns what the family thinks of the food. A meal with rot in it gets "That tastes off. Is it still fresh?" The letter grade sits behind a small Last meal toggle. On Day 20 the lockdown simply ends, and the report shows the days at home and each person's health.

media.caption: The report after Day 20.
The Day 5 paper reports medicine refills running late.
After dinner, one family member answers in a single line.

sections.summary: The phone has three channels: the city newspaper, the building group chat and the family chat. After each dinner one family member comments on the meal in a single line, usually the person who is doing worst. The letter grade is hidden behind a toggle. On Day 20 the lockdown ends and a report shows everyone's health.

sections.heading: Next
body: In the next build the knife slowly goes blunt. Hard ingredients wear it down faster, a blunt knife only cuts soft food like tofu or cabbage, and sharpening it depends on a neighbor lending a stone. Cut surfaces spoil faster than whole ingredients. On outage days the spoilage clock advances twice and the fridge hum cuts out.

Choices should also reach further. In that build the player picks which two items go to the 6F Stranger, and he comes back on Day 13 expecting the same deal. If Daughter was left to rest, her fever returns on Day 14. 7F sends something back on Day 17 only if they were helped. If the patrol catches the family on Day 18, no package arrives on Day 19.
sections.summary: The next build adds a knife that goes blunt, with a neighbour's sharpening stone to fix it, and cut surfaces that spoil faster than whole ingredients. Choices should also come back later: the sixth-floor stranger returns on Day 13 expecting the same deal, and a fever left untreated returns on Day 14.

download.label: Windows build v0.1.0 (Google Drive). Unzip and run LockDown.exe.

records.title: Trail Adventure
records.en: A first-person climbing and wildlife photography game
records.abstract: You inherit a cabin and a camera from Leo, an old photographer, on a mountain island with 24 animal species. Each trip starts by packing four tools at the cabin bench and ends at the summit, or when hunger, cold and tiredness have eaten the stamina bar. Any slope over 50 degrees can be climbed. Sixteen islanders ask for photos and send tools back by paper parachute.
findings: Climbing, running and jumping all spend one stamina bar. Hunger, cold, tiredness, injury and pack weight each shorten it.
A photo scores one to three stars from what is in the frame: distance, eye contact, flight, young, golden hour. Each species has a list of moments to collect.
The island, cave and mine are built by editor scripts, and the UI is drawn in code to look like a paper journal.

gallery.caption: Creeping up on deer by the pond

study.pitch: Trail Adventure is a first-person game. The player climbs a mountain island with an old camera and takes photos of the animals that live there. Most of the playing time goes into climbing. I made each animal hard to get to, so that the player remembers the climb and not only the photo.

sections.heading: Where it started
sections.summary: I started hiking after I moved to the United States for university, and the game comes from those trips. On Mount Rainier a ground squirrel sat on the rocks and looked straight at me, and higher up a marmot watched from a ridge in the fog. I only saw them because I had walked that far. So animals stay away from the path, climbing uses stamina, and a good photo takes patience.
body: I started hiking after I moved to the United States for university, and I usually had my camera with me. The game comes from those trips. Mount Rainier is the one I remember best. A ground squirrel sat on the rocks and looked straight at me. Higher up it was foggy, and a marmot was watching from a ridge. Both of them lived a long way up, and I only saw them because I had walked that far.

The basic rules of the game are taken from those trips. Animals stay away from the path, so the player has to climb to get to them. Climbing uses stamina. Animals leave once they notice the player, so a good photo usually takes patience.
A few of my photos are in the game too. They are the first pages of Leo's Journal.

media.caption: A ground squirrel on Mount Rainier, looking right at me.
A dolphin off Tampa.
Horseshoe Bend.

sections.heading: The first version
sections.summary: In the first version the player followed a fixed trail and rolled a die at each obstacle to get past. On a real mountain you stay on the trail, but in the game there was only walking between obstacles, and it was boring. Testing it, I mostly enjoyed running around photographing animals, and I remembered wanting to leave the trail at Antelope Canyon. So I removed the trails and the dice, and the mountain became the obstacle.
body: In the first version, the player followed a fixed trail with obstacles on it and rolled a die at each one to get past. I got this idea from real hiking, because on a real mountain you almost always stay on the trail. In the game, though, there was only walking between the obstacles, and it was boring.

While I was testing it, the part I enjoyed most was running around and taking photos of the animals. It also reminded me of Antelope Canyon in Arizona. When I was there I really wanted to leave the trail and walk out into the desert around it. So I decided to build the game around photography and let the player walk wherever they want.
I removed the trails and the dice. Now the player can climb anywhere on the mountain to look for animals, and the mountain is the obstacle.

media.caption: The October 11 build. A collapsed bridge: use a rope, or roll 5 or more to climb down.
Rolled a 2, minus 20 stamina. I checked out that build again to take these.
The trailhead in the October 11 build.

sections.heading: Climbing and stamina
sections.summary: Climbing is slow on purpose, about 0.6 meters a second, one pull at a time, with the hands kept low so they don't cover the rock. Running, climbing and jumping use stamina, but walking is free. Hunger, cold, injury, tiredness and a heavy bag each take a colored piece off the end of the bar. It is the only resource the player manages, the way being cold on a real hike just means less energy to climb.
body: Climbing is slow on purpose, about 0.6 meters a second. The player goes up one pull at a time, following the hands. I kept the hands low on the screen so they don't cover the rock or an animal sitting on it.
Running, climbing and jumping all use stamina, but walking is free, so that the player can look at the mountain and not at the bar.

Hunger, cold, injury, tiredness and a heavy bag each take a piece off the end of the bar, and each piece has its own color. I like it because I don't have to explain several systems to the player. The stamina bar is the only resource they have to manage, and every other effect is added on top of it. It is also how a real hike works, where being hungry or cold just means you have less energy to climb, and I think that helps the player feel they are really on the mountain.

media.caption: Going up a rock face one pull at a time.
Stamina bar at the Snow Fire, evening. Hunger and cold have each taken a slice.

sections.heading: Photography
sections.summary: Animals that haven't noticed anyone carry on with their own things, and every animal has moments worth a photo. A shot scores more if the animal is close, running or flying, or looking into the lens. Moving while shooting blurs the photo, which then scores half and can't be sent for a request. New photos earn stars, and stars upgrade the camera at the cabin bench, so good photos lead to better ones.
body: In real life, animals get scared when a person shows up. But when they haven't noticed anyone, they carry on with their own things, and every animal has moments of its own that are worth a photo. The scoring follows this. A photo gets more points if the animal is close, if it is running or flying, or if it is looking into the lens.

When I take photos while running, they come out shaky. I also didn't want the player to run up to an animal and take a quick shot, so moving while shooting blurs the photo. A blurred photo only gets half the score and can't be sent for a request.

New photos earn stars, and the player spends the stars at the bench in the cabin to upgrade the camera. I wanted photography to have a positive feedback loop. The more good photos the player takes, the better the camera gets, and with a better camera they can take more and better photos.

media.caption: The viewfinder right after a shot.
Fitting a new lens at the camera bench.

sections.heading: Animals
sections.summary: The animals I met on real trips didn't all react the same way, so all 24 species behave differently. When one notices the player it might stare, freeze, ignore her or walk closer, and when scared it might run, crouch, climb a tree or charge. Foxes steal snacks, goats spar, and the owl is out only from evening to morning. The field guide lists moments to photograph for each animal, and every new one gives a star.
body: The animals I met on real trips did not all react to me the same way. On Mount Rainier the ground squirrel sat and looked right at me, and the marmot kept watching from a ridge. So in the game all 24 species behave differently. When an animal notices the player, it might stare, freeze, ignore her or walk closer. When it gets scared, it might run, crouch, climb a tree or charge at her.

Some have habits of their own. Foxes steal snacks. Goats spar with each other and will butt anyone who gets too close. The ptarmigan hen won't leave her nest, and the owl is only out from early evening until morning. Sneaking lets the player get nearer before being noticed.

Each animal in the field guide has a list of moments to photograph, such as a close-up, on the run, or at night. Every new moment gives one star, so the player has a reason to go back to an animal they have already photographed.

media.caption: All 24 species, from the squirrel in the woods to the crayfish in the cave.
The fox's page in the field guide, with its moments listed.

sections.heading: Legendary creatures
sections.summary: Out in nature people often feel a mountain spirit might live there, so the island has nine legendary creatures taken from Chinese ink landscape paintings and old Chinese stories. Six live inside paintings: the player touches a scroll, ink covers the screen, and she is standing inside it. The other three are in the sky. The Wind Whale circles the island all day, and the Thunder Wyvern only appears after it starts raining.
body: When people are out in nature, they often feel that something like a mountain spirit might live there. I wanted the game to have that too, so the island has nine legendary creatures, taken from Chinese ink landscape paintings and old Chinese stories. They are very hard to find and hard to photograph well. Meeting one is a surprise, and it gives the player one more reason to keep climbing.

Six of them are inside paintings. The player touches a scroll, ink covers the screen, and when it clears she is standing inside the painting. Most of them come out of the mist to watch her, and go back into it if she gets too close.

The other three are in the sky. The Wind Whale circles the island over the sea all day. The Thunder Wyvern only appears after it starts raining, so the player has to pick a day with rain in the forecast.

media.caption: The Water Dragon, photographed inside its painting.
Concept painting for the Water Dragon's tarn.
The Branch Beast in its painting.

sections.heading: Requests
sections.summary: Sixteen people live on the island, each with a short story of two or three photo requests. The stories don't depend on each other, and every one of the 24 species is asked for at least once. All eight tools come from requests. Nell won't go into the dark cave, but says Shepherd Bram has a flashlight. The player photographs the ducks for him, and the Flashlight comes down by parachute.
body: Sixteen people live on the island. Each one has a short story of two or three photo requests. The stories don't depend on each other, so getting stuck on a hard request only stops that one story. I spread the requests so that every one of the 24 species is asked for at least once, and this takes the player all over the island.

Every request gives an item back, and all eight tools come from requests. So every tool the player gets has a small story behind it, and it doesn't feel like something she just picked up off the ground.

The Flashlight is an example. The cave is completely dark inside. Nell stands at the cave mouth and won't go in. When the player talks to her, she says that someone else on the island, Shepherd Bram, has a flashlight. The player goes to find Bram and takes a few photos for him, and then he gives her the Flashlight. With it she can go back and explore the whole cave.
points: Nell at the cave mouth.
Bram's last request: the ducks on the pond.
The ducks in the viewfinder.
The Flashlight comes down by parachute.
Down the mine ladder by flashlight.
Old Ida in the Miners' Camp.

media.caption: Nell at the cave mouth.
The Flashlight comes down by parachute.
Bram's last request: the ducks on the pond.
The ducks in the viewfinder.
Down the mine ladder by flashlight.
Old Ida in the Miners' Camp.

sections.heading: The cabin
sections.summary: When I get home from a real trip I have photos and a few small things from the way, so the cabin keeps those, and every trip starts and ends here. Stars buy camera upgrades at the bench, and a carving for the Carver's Shelf once every moment of a species is in the guide. The photo board holds favorite photos, finished stories send postcards, and the mail-order catalogue sells furniture.
body: When I get home from a real trip, I have photos and a few small things from the way. The cabin is where the game keeps those. Every trip starts and ends here.
The mail-order catalogue sells furniture and carvings for stars, so the camera is not the only thing stars can buy.
points: Camera bench. The player spends stars here to upgrade the camera.
Carver's Shelf. When every moment of a species is in the field guide, the player can order a carving of it.
Photo board. The player's favorite photos.
Postcard strings. When someone's story is finished, they send a postcard with a note on the back.
Wardrobe. The jackets hang here. Every tool has its own place in the cabin.
Packing bench. The player packs the bag here before a trip.

media.caption: The cabin: camera bench, Carver's Shelf, photo board, postcard strings, wardrobe and packing bench.
The mail-order catalogue sells furniture and carvings for stars.

sections.heading: Planning a trip
sections.summary: Before a trip the player makes a few choices in the cabin, so part of the day is decided when she walks out of the door. The window shows the weather, and cold or rain makes a jacket worth a place in the bag. Tools are packed at the bench by the door. On the wall map she starts at the trailhead or any fire she reached before. A roll is ten shots, and a new one only comes from resting at a fire.
body: Before a trip the player makes a few choices in the cabin. I put them there so that part of the day is already decided when she walks out of the door.
points: The weather. The window shows the weather for the day. If it says cold or rain, a jacket is worth a place in the bag.
Packing. The tools for the day are laid out on the bench by the door.
Where to start. On the wall map the player picks the trailhead or any fire she reached on an earlier trip.
Film. One roll is ten shots, and a new roll only comes from resting at a fire. The number at the bottom right of the viewfinder is how many shots are left.

media.caption: On the wall map the player picks the trailhead or any fire she reached on an earlier trip.
The window shows the weather for the day.
Packing the Flashlight at the bench by the door.
The number at the bottom right of the viewfinder is how many shots are left.

sections.heading: How to play
sections.summary: W, A, S and D to walk, Shift to run and C to sneak. Hold the left mouse button on rock to climb, and Space to jump or lunge up while climbing. The right mouse button raises the camera, the left takes the photo and the wheel zooms. R finds animals nearby, E is to talk, rest and use, Tab opens the phone and I opens the bag.
body: W A S D: walk. Shift: run. C: sneak.
Left mouse: hold on rock to climb. Space: jump, or lunge up while climbing.
Right mouse: raise the camera. Left mouse: take the photo. Scroll: zoom.
R: find animals nearby. E: talk, rest, use. Tab: phone, settings, quit. I: bag.

media.caption: The Wind Whale passing the mountain.

records.title: Last Mile
records.en: A management game about a food-delivery station
records.abstract: You manage Lanting, a small food-delivery station, for ten days. Orders appear on a 3D map of the district as countdown pins, and you assign each one to a rider, a ground robot or a drone. Riders are paid per drop, and each of them needs money for something by a certain day. From Day 3 headquarters starts adding machines, and each one takes a rider's place on the roster.
findings: Every order is assigned by hand. The deadline is set from the fastest available courier, so a late order is usually the result of a dispatch decision.
Four riders each have one bill due on a set day, and an even share of the orders is just enough to cover it.
The district is a road graph based on Xujiahui, filled in by editor scripts. A headless test plays all ten days and checks that all 132 orders resolve.

gallery.caption: Orders as countdown pins over the city

study.pitch: A ten-day management game about a small food-delivery station. Orders land on the map as countdown pins and you decide who takes each one: a rider paid per drop, a ground robot or a drone.

sections.heading: The orders
body: The riders are paid by the drop, so sending Chen instead of Xiaoyu on an ID check decides which of them gets closer to the bill they are saving for. Over the ten days headquarters moves the station onto robots and drones.

The first version was a policy game with sliders for pay and late fees, and a pay cut was spread over everyone, so nobody in particular lost anything. I changed it so the player hands out every order by hand to riders with names.
points: The board counts parcels, so a crate counts the same as a coffee.
Each machine fixes one problem and leaves another.
AO-6, the assistant from day 6, never overrules the player.
sections.summary: The first version was a policy game with sliders for pay and late fees. A pay cut was spread across everyone, so nobody in particular was affected. I rewrote it so that every order is assigned by hand to a rider with a name. Riders are paid per drop, so giving an ID-check order to Chen rather than Xiaoyu changes who gets closer to paying their bill.

media.caption: The title screen: the desk in the depot, with Zhou Heng's first text on the phone.

sections.heading: A day
body: The station gets ¥180 each morning. The player can save it, or spend ¥80 to coach the rider who knows the streets least, ¥90 on breakfast and a rest, or ¥50 to add 15 seconds to the first four orders.

A shift is two 90-second waves. On day 1 six orders arrive one at a time. From day 2 each wave opens with two orders and the rest land in a burst from 36 seconds in, while the first riders are still out, so someone has to wait. Orders rise to 16 a day by day 7. Between waves the player can pay ¥40 for 20 more seconds on new orders, or take ¥60 of rush money that cuts 15 seconds and adds one to the target.

Each rider costs ¥30 in wages at night. The report puts delivered against target next to what each rider took home, so a good day for the station and a bad day for one rider sit on the same page. A station that can't pay wages closes, and the player replays that morning.

media.caption: One day, from the GDD.
Day 4 morning on the phone.
The day 4 report: 12 delivered against a target of 10, and each rider's pay.

sections.summary: Each morning the station gets ¥180 to save or spend: ¥80 to coach the newest rider, ¥90 for breakfast and rest, ¥50 for extra time on the first orders. A shift is two 90-second waves. Day 1 has six orders; by Day 7 there are 16. Each rider costs ¥30 in wages at night. The evening report shows deliveries against target next to each rider's earnings, and a station that cannot pay wages closes.

sections.heading: Dispatch
body: Clicking a pin lists who could take the order, with an arrival estimate. A card for someone who can't go is locked and says why, and the clock holds until the player chooses.

The deadline comes from the fastest rested courier on the ground who could take the order, times about 1.4 on day 2 and 1.2 by day 10. I based it on the best courier so that a slower pick, or an order left waiting, is what makes it late. Orders cancel 25 seconds after the deadline.

Each drop costs a rider 8 stamina on top of the ride, and a tired rider slows to 70% speed. Rest gives 12 seconds off and about 36 stamina. Waiting at the station gives nothing, so a break is something the manager has to give.
points: Standard: anyone. ¥6 to the station, ¥4 to the rider.
ID check: a rider, or from day 8 a robot with an ¥80 scanner. ¥8 and ¥5.
Sixth floor, no lift: a rider or a drone. ¥8 and ¥5.
Heavy restock: Strength 8. ¥10 and ¥6. A late drop halves both.

media.caption: Day 4: a breakfast for a building with no lift. The robot is locked out.

sections.summary: Click a pin to see who can take the order and when they would arrive. Couriers who cannot do it are greyed out with the reason, and the clock waits until you choose. The deadline is calculated from the fastest rested courier, times 1.4 on Day 2 and 1.2 by Day 10, so a slower pick or a delay is what makes it late. Each drop costs a rider 8 stamina, and a tired rider moves at 70% speed.

sections.heading: The machines
body: The robot arrives on day 3. It is never paid per drop, but it can't climb stairs or check an ID. That night headquarters compares it with the riders on standard orders. If the riders were on time more often, the player can send it back. A tie goes to the robot.

The drone comes on day 4. It flies straight over the blocks and is the fastest courier on the map, but it carries a load of 5 at most. If the robot stayed, headquarters wants 2 machines on the roster from day 6, 3 from day 8 and 4 on day 10, out of six places, so every machine takes a rider's place.

From day 6 AO-6 recommends someone for every order. Each Confirm, or each time the player picks someone else, is saved as an example. It keeps the last 96 and cites them: "This follows what you did on Day 6, #1058." I wanted the player to train it willingly, one Confirm at a time.

media.caption: How AO-6 learns: each Confirm or override is saved as an example.

sections.summary: The robot arrives on Day 3. It isn't paid per drop but can't climb stairs or check ID. That night headquarters compares it with the riders on standard orders, and if the riders did better you can send it back. The drone comes on Day 4, fastest on the map, with a load of 5. From Day 6, AO-6 suggests a courier for every order and learns from each confirm or override, keeping the last 96 as examples. It never overrides you.

sections.heading: The riders
body: Each rider has three scores out of 10: Streets for speed, Strength for load, Judgment for tricky handovers. Chen is 9, 4 and 9. Ajie is 5, 9 and 5. Lin is 8, 6 and 6. Xiaoyu joins on day 2 at 4, 6 and 8.

Each is short of money for one thing by one evening: Xiaoyu ¥30 for a room deposit by day 4, Lin ¥40 rent by day 5, Ajie ¥50 he owes a friend by day 6, Chen ¥80 for his wife's medicine by day 9. A fair share of the work just covers it. On the evening her deposit is due, Xiaoyu asks for an order and stops halfway: "Could I... sorry. Could I take this one?" If she falls short she loses the room and starts every shift 20 seconds late.

From day 2 one rider calls each evening about something the board doesn't count. Ajie asks for small parcels, because "the board counts parcels, not weight." I kept one rule for the writing: the riders talk about crates, rent and doorbells, and only AO-6 and headquarters carry the satire.

media.caption: Day 4: Xiaoyu asks for an order on the evening her deposit is due.
Lin asks to skip the evening rush to pick up his daughter.

sections.summary: Each rider has three scores out of 10 for streets, strength and judgment. Chen is 9, 4, 9; Ajie 5, 9, 5; Lin 8, 6, 6; Xiaoyu, who joins on Day 2, is 4, 6, 8. Each has one bill due: Xiaoyu ¥30 for a room deposit by Day 4, Lin ¥40 rent by Day 5, Ajie ¥50 owed to a friend by Day 6, Chen ¥80 for his wife's medicine by Day 9. From Day 2 one rider calls every evening about something the board does not count.

sections.heading: The district
body: The map is modelled on Xujiahui: 26 hand-placed junctions around a six-armed crossing, with eight outer districts generated as five-by-five street grids. Orders go to four of them, among them Willow Bend and Heron Road.

An editor script finds each closed block in the road graph, lines its edges with lots and fills the middle with a grid turned to the longest side. The ordinary buildings are built in code. The landmarks and vehicles are AI-generated models that editor scripts fit into the blocks.
The light follows the shift from warm morning to blue evening, but the interface keeps its colours, so a red countdown at dusk looks the same as one at breakfast.

media.caption: The rain alert on day 4, over the map.
Ajie calls about a moved drop-off.

sections.summary: The map is based on Xujiahui: 26 hand-placed junctions around a six-way crossing, with eight outer districts generated as 5 by 5 grids. An editor script finds each closed block in the road graph, lines it with lots and fills the middle. The ordinary buildings are generated in code; the landmarks and vehicles are AI-generated models placed by script. Lighting goes from warm morning to blue evening, but the UI colours stay fixed.

sections.heading: Teaching and testing
body: Day 1 teaches by doing. Zhou Heng, the regional manager, walks the player through the first dispatch, and later lessons appear the first time they are needed, such as Strength on the first full crate.

The editor can also play the trial by itself. A scripted manager runs all ten days on the real roads and traffic, and the run fails if any of the 132 orders doesn't end in a delivery or a cancellation, if traffic stops, if two bodies overlap, or if a story call is left open.

media.caption: The ticket before the evening wave: keep it standard, buy extra time or take rush pay.

In the editor a scripted manager can play all ten days on the real roads. The test fails if any of the 132 orders does not end in a delivery or a cancellation, if traffic deadlocks, if two bodies overlap, or if a story call is left open.

records.title: Sniff & Snitch
records.en: A two-player online co-op stealth game
records.abstract: Two players break out of a magic prison together, one as Lyra, a witch, and one as Fia, a red panda. Routes split where one of them can pass and the other can't, and doors, boxes and takedowns need both. Guards see in a 120-degree cone and hear through walls. A caught player is taken to a gas cage, and the partner has 15 seconds to open it. Capstone team project; I'm a programmer and designer on it.
findings: Guards are state machines with 18 states. They see 12.3 m in a 120-degree cone and hear through walls, with each wall halving a sound past its first 5 m.
A caught player is walked to a gas cage. The partner has 15 seconds to reach it and hold E for 1.5 seconds.
Doors, push boxes, the lift gate and the takedown need both players. The server only syncs who is gripping, tap counts and start times; animations are computed locally.

study.pitch: An online co-op stealth game for two. Lyra, a witch, and Fia, a red panda, break out of a magic prison together. I'm a programmer and designer on the capstone team, and I built the guard AI, the capture and rescue loop and most of the two-player mechanisms.

facts.label: Engine
facts.value: Unity 6, C#, Netcode for GameObjects, Unity Relay

sections.heading: Lyra and Fia
body: Lyra and Fia are both in for theft, and neither of them gets out of the prison alone. Each player claims one of them on the character select screen, and the run starts once both roles are taken.

We built the two of them to be good at different things. Lyra is 1.8 m tall, drags boxes, and can put on a mask that keeps guards from growing suspicious of her. Fia is 1.0 m tall, jumps 1.4 m to Lyra's 1.0, climbs ledges and can dash 3.5 m. Some magic barriers stop only one of them, marked with a paw or a witch icon, so most rooms have a route for each.

media.caption: Character select: each player picks a mugshot card.
Fia's mugshot card on the character select screen.

sections.summary: Each player picks one character and the run starts when both are taken. Lyra is 1.8 m tall, can drag boxes, and can wear a mask that stops guards getting suspicious. Fia is 1.0 m, jumps 1.4 m to Lyra's 1.0, climbs ledges and dashes 3.5 m. Some magic barriers only block one of them, marked with a paw or a witch icon, so most rooms have a separate route for each.

sections.heading: Meeting up
body: The first stretch of Level 1 gives Lyra and Fia a "Find a way out" step each. The two run in parallel, and only when both are done does the next step appear: "Meet at the door".

Each character also has an exit of their own, and the level is won only when both players are standing in theirs. A checkpoint saves only after every connected player has walked into it, so a restart always brings the two of them back to the same checkpoint.

media.caption: The success screen, shown when both players reach their exits.

sections.summary: The start of Level 1 gives each character their own "find a way out" objective. They run in parallel, and only when both are done does the next one appear: meet at the door. Each character also has their own exit, and the level is only complete when both are standing in theirs. Checkpoints save when every connected player has reached them.

sections.heading: Guards
body: I built the guard AI. Each guard is one state machine with 18 states and a suspicion meter from 0 to 1. He sees 12.3 m in a 120 degree cone. An unmasked player within 2.8 m fills the meter in one second, and at the edge of his sight in about 1.8 seconds.

Hearing is a separate system. Crouching carries 4 m, walking 10 m and running 16 m. The first 5 m of a sound pass through walls at full strength, and each wall after that halves what is left, so Fia running behind one wall is heard out to 10.5 m instead of 16.

A noise can pull a guard off his patrol, but it cannot interrupt a guard who is already watching someone. I set it up this way so a thrown coin has to be planned before a guard looks at you; once he is watching, it does nothing.
sections.summary: I built the guard AI. Each guard is a state machine with 18 states and a suspicion meter. He sees 12.3 m in a 120-degree cone, and an unmasked player within 2.8 m fills the meter in a second. Hearing is separate: crouching carries 4 m, walking 10, running 16, and each wall past the first 5 m halves the sound. A noise can pull a guard off patrol but not off a player he is already watching.

sections.heading: The cage
body: Getting caught does not end the run. The guard cuffs the player and walks them to his cage. During the escort their camera sits 35 degrees off the guard's right shoulder, because from straight behind, the guard hides the player walking in front of him.

In the cage, green gas thickens as time runs down. The partner has 15 seconds to get there and hold E for 1.5 seconds. Opening the lock makes a 14 m noise, and for 20 seconds any guard who sees the empty cage comes to check. When Fia frees Lyra with the gas nearly full, the clang of the lock turns the nearest guard toward them as they run.

If the time runs out, or a guard catches the second player while the first is still held, the level ends for both. I built the cage HUD for the free player: a cage icon tracks the partner across the screen and flashes faster as time runs out.

media.caption: The game over screen when the partner is not rescued in time.
Fia's game over card: "You have been captured."

sections.summary: Being caught doesn't end the run. The guard cuffs you and walks you to his cage, where gas fills up over 15 seconds. Your partner has that long to reach the cage and hold E for 1.5 seconds. Opening the lock makes a 14 m noise, and for 20 seconds any guard who sees the empty cage comes to check. If time runs out, or the second player is caught too, the level ends for both.

sections.heading: Doors and boxes
body: The latch door has one lever locked to Lyra and one to Fia, and opens only while both are down. The push box has a handle for each at their own height. Once both have grabbed, either player's W fills one shared ring, and ten taps slide the box 2.5 m. Pushed off a ledge, it becomes a step, and the landing reaches guards 25 m away. The lift door is a heavy gate they raise together, walk under, and let slam shut behind them for good.

The takedown needs both players too. A masked Lyra presses a seal onto an unaware guard, which weakens him for 6 seconds. In that window Fia drops onto him from at least 1.4 m above, and he is out for 12 seconds unless another guard walks up and wakes him.

For these mechanisms the server writes only who is gripping, how many taps have landed and when a sequence starts. Each machine works out the door height and the players' animations from that start time, so a player who joins late sees the same door and no animation has to be sent.
sections.summary: The latch door has a lever for each character and opens only while both are held down. The push box has a handle at each height; once both have grabbed it, ten taps of W move it 2.5 m. For the takedown, a masked Lyra marks a guard, then Fia drops on him from above 1.4 m. The server only syncs who is gripping, how many taps have landed and when a sequence started. Each client computes the door height and the animations from that.

sections.heading: Pings and throws
body: Middle mouse drops a ping on whatever is under the crosshair. Each player has one ping at a time, and it lasts 8 seconds. A ping on a guard sticks to him and moves with him, so the partner knows which guard is meant after he turns a corner.

Holding E lifts a crate overhead. A tap of the left mouse button tosses it 4 m, and holding for half a second throws it 8 m. The crate sits a set height above each character's own head, because a height measured on Lyra left Fia's crate floating a metre above her.

A teammate set up the first quest data and HUD. I turned each level's quests into node graphs of reach, interact and acquire steps, each assigned to Lyra, Fia, either or both, with the server deciding who completed each step. Character select is server-owned as well, and a player who drops out mid-level rejoins in whichever role is free.
sections.summary: Middle mouse puts a ping on whatever is under the crosshair for 8 seconds, and a ping on a guard follows him. Holding E lifts a crate; a tap throws it 4 m, a half-second hold 8 m. The crate height is relative to each character, because a height set for Lyra left Fia's crate floating a metre above her head. I also rebuilt the quest system as node graphs of reach, interact and acquire steps, each assigned to Lyra, Fia, either or both.

sections.heading: Next
body: Coins still use an older flat noise radius that ignores walls, and I want them on the same hearing model as footsteps. Lyra and Fia have separate entries in the noise table with the same values, and quieter steps for Fia would give the players a reason to send her ahead.

Every guard has a hearing multiplier, set to 1 in the current levels; I want to use it for a guard dog at 2.5. I also built a slow curse for guards who cannot reach a player, which slows the player to 45% speed for 3.5 seconds, and I want to place it where a player can stand out of reach.
sections.summary: Coins still use a flat noise radius that ignores walls, and they should use the same hearing model as footsteps. Fia's footsteps should be quieter than Lyra's, to give a reason to send her ahead. Every guard has a hearing multiplier, currently 1, which I want to use for a guard dog at 2.5.
